idiom_name: html/template actions, model fetched in the handler
implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies the engine but not the scriptlet: text/template and html/template give pipelines, if/range/with and method calls on the data, and a template is escaped as a whole before Execute, which is why a template cannot be parsed after it has been executed. Model access therefore stays in the handler, which fetches the data and hands it to Execute, so Go keeps only the template half of the pattern and moves the 'the view fetches its own data' half out of the view; calling a repository from inside a template requires registering functions and goes against the grain. The idiomatic shape is parse once at startup and execute per request with a small data struct; fmt.Fprintf handlers remain justified for tiny fixed responses where a template file is more machinery than the page.
pitfalls: Passing template.HTML or the template.HTMLAttr type marks a value as already safe and disables escaping - the same hole as Razor's Raw, one type assertion away.
html/template cannot Parse after Execute, so per-request template parsing or post-processing fails with an error rather than re-escaping; load templates once at startup.
Contextual escaping is per action position: the same value used inside a script or CSS context needs a different escaping and pre-assembling strings before insertion defeats the analysis.
Executing to a shared http.ResponseWriter writes partial output before a nested template error is returned, so failures leave a truncated page rather than a clean error status.
